Debut year of these famous characters.Mickey Mouse: Mickey debuted in Steamboat Willie, one of the first cartoons with synchronized sound, after Walt Disney lost the rights to Oswald the Lucky Rabbit.
Debut year of these famous characters.Superman: His first comic appearance in Action Comics number 1 launched the superhero genre, and a copy has sold for millions of dollars.
Debut year of these famous characters.Bugs Bunny: The wisecracking rabbit's what's up, Doc debuted in A Wild Hare, and he became Warner Bros.' biggest star.
Debut year of these famous characters.Kermit the Frog: Jim Henson made the first Kermit from his mother's old coat and ping-pong balls, and he began as a vague lizard-like creature.
Debut year of these famous characters.Spider-Man: Stan Lee wanted a teenage hero with everyday problems, and Spidey's first appearance was in Amazing Fantasy 15, in a series about to be canceled.
Debut year of these famous characters.Hello Kitty: Sanrio's cat is officially a little girl from London, and she has no mouth so people can project their own feelings.
Debut year of these famous characters.Pac-Man: Designer Toru Iwatani says the shape came from a pizza with a slice missing, and the game was first named Puck-Man.
Debut year of these famous characters.Mario: He first appeared as Jumpman, and was renamed after Mario Segale, the landlord of Nintendo of America's warehouse.
Debut year of these famous characters.Pikachu: His name blends pika for sparkle and chu for a mouse's squeak, and he became the face of Pokemon.
Debut year of these famous characters.SpongeBob SquarePants: Created by marine biologist and animator Stephen Hillenburg, the show has run for over twenty five years.

Ancient Greece, in chronological order.First Olympic Games: Traditionally dated to 776 BC, the first Games at Olympia had just one event, a footrace of about 190 meters.
Ancient Greece, in chronological order.Solon's reforms in Athens: Solon canceled debts and banned loans secured on a person's own freedom, easing a crisis that had pushed poor Athenians toward slavery.
Ancient Greece, in chronological order.Cleisthenes' democracy: Called the father of Athenian democracy, Cleisthenes redrew the citizens into ten new tribes, weakening the old aristocratic clans.
Ancient Greece, in chronological order.Battle of Salamis: Themistocles lured the much larger Persian fleet into the narrow straits near Athens, where the nimbler Greek triremes won a famous victory.
Ancient Greece, in chronological order.Parthenon begun: Pericles launched the temple to Athena, built mostly within about nine years. In 1687 a Venetian shell hit gunpowder stored inside.
Ancient Greece, in chronological order.Peloponnesian War begins: The 27-year struggle between Athens and Sparta was recorded by the historian Thucydides, who had himself served as a general.
Ancient Greece, in chronological order.Socrates executed: Convicted of impiety and of corrupting the young, Socrates drank hemlock. We know him mostly through his student Plato.
Ancient Greece, in chronological order.Battle of Chaeronea: Philip II of Macedon crushed Athens and Thebes here. His teenage son Alexander commanded a cavalry wing in the battle.
Ancient Greece, in chronological order.Alexander the Great dies: Alexander died in Babylon aged about 32, and the cause, fever, poison or something else, is still debated.
Ancient Greece, in chronological order.Rome sacks Corinth: Rome destroyed Corinth in the same year as Carthage, and Greece soon became a Roman province.

Poets, by birth year.Sappho: Few of Sappho's poems survive, mostly in fragments, yet she was so admired that Plato called her the tenth Muse.
Poets, by birth year.Virgil: Rome's national poet wrote the Aeneid, which he reportedly wanted burned on his deathbed, but Augustus saved it.
Poets, by birth year.Rumi: This Persian poet and Sufi mystic is often called the bestselling poet in America, thanks to translations of his verse.
Poets, by birth year.Petrarch: This Italian scholar and poet gave Europe the sonnet form, and is often called the father of humanism.
Poets, by birth year.Matsuo Bashō: The Japanese master of haiku, who travelled across Japan on foot, wrote the travel journal The Narrow Road to the Deep North.
Poets, by birth year.William Blake: Blake was also a painter and engraver, and he printed his own illustrated books such as Songs of Innocence and of Experience.
Poets, by birth year.Emily Dickinson: Only a handful of her poems were published in her lifetime, and almost 1,800 were found in her bedroom after her death.
Poets, by birth year.Rainer Maria Rilke: Rilke wrote Letters to a Young Poet and the Duino Elegies, and his poems about solitude and transformation remain widely read.
Poets, by birth year.Pablo Neruda: This Chilean poet won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1971, and wrote Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair as a young man.
Poets, by birth year.Sylvia Plath: Her only novel, The Bell Jar, and her posthumous collection Ariel made her one of the best-known confessional poets.

Christmas stories, by first publication.The Nutcracker and Mouse King: E.T.A. Hoffmann's darker tale inspired Tchaikovsky's ballet, which cleaned up the story for the stage.
Christmas stories, by first publication.The Night Before Christmas: Published anonymously, the poem gave Santa his eight reindeer names, and is usually credited to Clement Clarke Moore.
Christmas stories, by first publication.A Christmas Carol: Dickens wrote it in about six weeks, and its first printing sold out within days of Christmas 1843.
Christmas stories, by first publication.The Little Match Girl: Hans Christian Andersen's story ends sadly, with the girl freezing in the snow, which is not the stuff of cozy holiday cheer.
Christmas stories, by first publication.Yes, Virginia (editorial): The newspaper answered an 8-year-old girl's question about Santa, and is among the most reprinted editorials in English.
Christmas stories, by first publication.The Gift of the Magi: O. Henry's short story is built on a twist: a poor couple each sell their treasure to buy the other a gift.
Christmas stories, by first publication.Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer: Robert May created him for a department store's free booklet, and his brother-in-law Johnny Marks turned it into a hit song.
Christmas stories, by first publication.How the Grinch Stole Christmas: Dr. Seuss wrote it as his own gripe about the holiday, and Boris Karloff later voiced the Grinch in the 1966 TV special.
Christmas stories, by first publication.The Snowman (Briggs): Raymond Briggs's wordless picture book became a beloved 1982 animated film with the song Walking in the Air.
Christmas stories, by first publication.The Polar Express: Chris Van Allsburg's tale of a train to the North Pole won the Caldecott Medal, and a bell only believers can hear.

Weather science milestones, in order.Galileo's thermoscope: Galileo's device showed temperature changes through a rising and falling water level, but had no scale to measure them.
Weather science milestones, in order.Torricelli's barometer: Evangelista Torricelli filled a glass tube with mercury and upended it, showing that air has weight and pressure.
Weather science milestones, in order.Fahrenheit's scale: Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit based his scale on a freezing brine mixture and body temperature, and used mercury in the thermometer.
Weather science milestones, in order.Celsius's scale: The original scale was inverted, with 0 for boiling and 100 for freezing, and it was flipped after his death.
Weather science milestones, in order.Luke Howard names the clouds: Luke Howard gave us cirrus, cumulus and stratus in a Latin system; Goethe even wrote poems about the names.
Weather science milestones, in order.Cup anemometer invented: It was invented by Irish astronomer Thomas Romney Robinson, and cups catch the wind to measure its speed.
Weather science milestones, in order.UK Met Office founded: It was founded by Robert FitzRoy, captain of the Beagle on Darwin's voyage, and he coined the term 'forecast'.
Weather science milestones, in order.US hurricanes get names: Storms were named for women at first, and men's names were added in 1979 to even things out.
Weather science milestones, in order.First weather satellite: TIROS-1 was launched in April 1960 and sent back the first television pictures of cloud patterns from space.
Weather science milestones, in order.Fujita tornado scale: Ted Fujita's F0 to F5 scale ranked tornadoes by damage, and was replaced by the Enhanced Fujita scale in 2007.

Word games and shows, by debut year.The crossword puzzle: Arthur Wynne's Word-cross ran in the New York World on 21 December 1913, in a diamond shape with no black squares.
Word games and shows, by debut year.Scripps Spelling Bee: The Louisville Courier-Journal started it in 1925; the first national champion won by spelling gladiolus.
Word games and shows, by debut year.Scrabble: Alfred Butts invented it in the 1930s under other names; James Brunot renamed it Scrabble in 1948.
Word games and shows, by debut year.Jumble: Henri Arnold and Martin Naydel created it, and it is among the longest-running newspaper puzzles.
Word games and shows, by debut year.Boggle: Allan Turoff invented it and Parker Brothers sold it; players shake a grid of sixteen letter cubes.
Word games and shows, by debut year.Wheel of Fortune: Created by Merv Griffin, who also created Jeopardy!, it began on NBC in 1975.
Word games and shows, by debut year.Countdown (UK TV): Its first episode in 1982 opened Channel 4, which launched on 2 November that year.
Word games and shows, by debut year.Bananagrams: Created by Abraham Nathanson, it ships in a banana-shaped pouch.
Word games and shows, by debut year.Codenames: Vlaada Chvatil designed it, and it won the 2016 Spiel des Jahres.
Word games and shows, by debut year.Wordle: Josh Wardle created it for his partner, and the New York Times bought it in 2022.

Dog breeds by weight.Chihuahua: Named for the Mexican state of Chihuahua, it is the smallest breed, yet it is thought to descend from the Techichi.
Dog breeds by weight.Yorkshire terrier: It was bred in Yorkshire mills to catch rats, and its silky coat is much like human hair.
Dog breeds by weight.Pug: Pugs were favoured by Chinese emperors and by the Dutch royal family; a group of pugs is called a grumble.
Dog breeds by weight.Beagle: Beagles have around 220 million scent receptors, hundreds of millions, which is why they sniff out fruit at airports.
Dog breeds by weight.Cocker spaniel: The name comes from hunting woodcock, and Lady in Lady and the Tramp was one.
Dog breeds by weight.Border collie: Border collies often rank as the smartest breed; one named Chaser learned over a thousand words.
Dog breeds by weight.Standard poodle: Originally a water retriever in Germany, its show clip once protected its joints.
Dog breeds by weight.German shepherd: Created by Max von Stephanitz in 1899 for herding, it is now a common police dog.
Dog breeds by weight.Newfoundland: Webbed feet and a water-repellent coat make it a natural rescuer, and it has saved swimmers.
Dog breeds by weight.English mastiff: An English mastiff named Zorba weighed 155 kg in 1987, the heaviest dog on record.

When these phone and casual games came o.Snake (Nokia): Snake came preloaded on Nokia phones, and it was played by hundreds of millions of people.
When these phone and casual games came o.Bejeweled: Bejeweled's match-three gameplay was a huge hit, and it was one of the first casual games to take off.
When these phone and casual games came o.Doodle Jump: Doodle Jump was made by two brothers, and it made tilting a phone a standard way to play.
When these phone and casual games came o.Fruit Ninja: Fruit Ninja lets players slice flying fruit with a finger, and it has been downloaded over a billion times.
When these phone and casual games came o.Temple Run: Temple Run popularized the endless runner, and it was downloaded millions of times in its first weeks.
When these phone and casual games came o.Flappy Bird: Flappy Bird was created by a Vietnamese developer, who pulled it from app stores at its peak because it was too addictive.
When these phone and casual games came o.Monument Valley: Monument Valley is a puzzle game based on impossible architecture like Escher's drawings, and it won design awards.
When these phone and casual games came o.Pokémon Go: Pokemon Go had people walking outside to catch creatures, and it was downloaded over 500 million times in its first year.
When these phone and casual games came o.Among Us: Among Us was released in 2018 but only became a sensation in 2020, thanks to streamers and lockdowns.
When these phone and casual games came o.Wordle: Wordle was created by Josh Wardle for his partner, and The New York Times bought it in 2022 for a seven-figure sum.

When these airports opened.Amsterdam Schiphol: Founded as a military airfield, it lies about 3 m below sea level, built on drained land that was once a lake.
When these airports opened.London Heathrow: It began as a small airfield in the 1930s, and in 1946 passengers walked into tents that served as terminals.
When these airports opened.New York JFK (Idlewild): Originally named Idlewild, it was renamed in 1963 after the assassinated president John F. Kennedy.
When these airports opened.Washington Dulles: The swooping, curved roof designed by Eero Saarinen makes the terminal look like it is about to take off.
When these airports opened.Paris Charles de Gaulle: Terminal 1 is a round concrete building, nicknamed the Camembert, with tubes crossing its center.
When these airports opened.Tokyo Narita: Local farmers and activists protested for years over land taken for it, and clashes continued even after it opened.
When these airports opened.Singapore Changi: Regularly rated the world's best airport, it has an indoor waterfall, butterfly garden and cinema.
When these airports opened.Denver International: Famously, an automated baggage system failed so badly that opening was delayed by 16 months; it is among the largest in area.
When these airports opened.Hong Kong Chek Lap Kok: It replaced the old Kai Tak, whose approach over crowded rooftops was famous, and sits on an artificially flattened island.
When these airports opened.Beijing Daxing: Designed by Zaha Hadid, its starfish-shaped terminal is one of the largest single-building airport terminals in the world.

Discoveries about the body and its cells.Blood circulation (Harvey): William Harvey showed the heart pumps blood in a circuit, overturning Galen's ideas that had stood for some 1,400 years.
Discoveries about the body and its cells.Cells named (Hooke): Robert Hooke saw box-like compartments in thin cork under his microscope and named them cells after monks' small rooms.
Discoveries about the body and its cells.Bacteria first seen: Dutch cloth merchant Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground his own lenses and called the tiny creatures he saw animalcules.
Discoveries about the body and its cells.Cell theory: Schleiden and Schwann concluded all living things are made of cells, and Virchow later added that new cells come from existing ones.
Discoveries about the body and its cells.DNA first isolated: Swiss chemist Friedrich Miescher extracted it from pus-soaked bandages and called it nuclein, decades before anyone knew its role.
Discoveries about the body and its cells.Neurons as units (Cajal): Santiago Ramon y Cajal's drawings showed the brain is made of separate cells, earning him a 1906 Nobel Prize shared with Golgi.
Discoveries about the body and its cells.Blood groups: Karl Landsteiner's discovery of the ABO groups made safe transfusion possible and won him the 1930 Nobel Prize.
Discoveries about the body and its cells.Vitamins proposed (Funk): Casimir Funk coined vitamine for nutrients that prevent diseases like beriberi, and the final e was later dropped.
Discoveries about the body and its cells.Krebs cycle: Hans Krebs described the cycle of reactions by which cells draw energy from food, winning the 1953 Nobel Prize.
Discoveries about the body and its cells.First genetic codon cracked: Nirenberg and Matthaei showed that the codon UUU codes for phenylalanine, the first step in cracking the genetic code.

Bones from head to toe.Parietal: Two of them form the roof and sides of the skull, meeting at the sagittal suture.
Bones from head to toe.Mandible: It is the only movable bone of the skull, apart from the tiny bones of the ear.
Bones from head to toe.Hyoid: This U-shaped bone connects to no other bone, anchors the tongue, and a fracture can signal strangulation.
Bones from head to toe.Clavicle: It is the most commonly broken bone in children, and the only long bone lying horizontally.
Bones from head to toe.Sternum: It has three parts, the manubrium, body and xiphoid process.
Bones from head to toe.Lumbar vertebrae: Five of these, the largest in the spine, carry most of the body's weight.
Bones from head to toe.Femur: It is the longest and strongest bone in the body.
Bones from head to toe.Patella: This sesamoid bone sits inside a tendon, and in babies it is still mostly cartilage.
Bones from head to toe.Tibia: This weight-bearing shin bone is the second-longest bone in the body.
Bones from head to toe.Calcaneus: It is the largest tarsal bone, and the Achilles tendon attaches to it.

Modern artists, by birth year.Gustav Klimt: Klimt led the Vienna Secession and painted gold-leaf works like The Kiss, which was inspired by Byzantine mosaics he saw in Ravenna.
Modern artists, by birth year.Wassily Kandinsky: Kandinsky, a Russian-born artist, is often called a pioneer of abstract art, and he also drew on his sense of music for his titles.
Modern artists, by birth year.Henri Matisse: Matisse led Fauvism, the 'wild beasts' movement, and in old age he made colorful paper cut-outs when illness kept him in bed or a wheelchair.
Modern artists, by birth year.Pablo Picasso: Picasso co-founded Cubism with Georges Braque and was prolific, producing an estimated 50,000 artworks in his lifetime.
Modern artists, by birth year.René Magritte: The Belgian Surrealist painted The Treachery of Images, a pipe captioned 'This is not a pipe', and often wore a bowler hat.
Modern artists, by birth year.Salvador Dalí: Dalí's melting clocks in The Persistence of Memory were reportedly inspired by Camembert cheese melting in the sun.
Modern artists, by birth year.Jackson Pollock: Pollock poured and dripped paint onto canvases laid on the floor, and his 'action painting' made him a leader of Abstract Expressionism.
Modern artists, by birth year.Roy Lichtenstein: Lichtenstein enlarged comic-book panels, down to the Ben-Day dots, and he used them to create Pop Art classics such as Drowning Girl.
Modern artists, by birth year.Andy Warhol: Warhol said he wanted to be a machine, and his Factory studio turned out silkscreened soup cans and celebrity portraits in series.
Modern artists, by birth year.Jean-Michel Basquiat: Basquiat began as a graffiti artist tagging SAMO, and one of his paintings was sold in 2017 for over 110 million dollars.

Dickens novels, by when serialization be.The Pickwick Papers: Dickens's first novel appeared in monthly parts in 1836, and its Sam Weller character boosted sales from a few hundred copies to some 40,000 an issue.
Dickens novels, by when serialization be.Oliver Twist: This story of an orphan in a workhouse, who asked 'Please, sir, I want some more', was serialized in a magazine called Bentley's Miscellany.
Dickens novels, by when serialization be.The Old Curiosity Shop: Dickens's story of Little Nell was so popular that crowds in New York reportedly waited at the docks to ask arriving sailors if she was dead.
Dickens novels, by when serialization be.A Christmas Carol: Written in six weeks, this novella gave us 'Bah! Humbug!' and helped shape the modern idea of a family Christmas.
Dickens novels, by when serialization be.David Copperfield: The author drew from his own boyhood work in a blacking warehouse for this novel, which he called his 'favorite child'.
Dickens novels, by when serialization be.Bleak House: This tale centers on the endless court case Jarndyce and Jarndyce, a satire of the slow Chancery system, and it opens with a famous fog description.
Dickens novels, by when serialization be.Hard Times: Dickens's shortest novel, set in the fictional Coketown, was a critique of the industrial age's focus on facts and figures.
Dickens novels, by when serialization be.A Tale of Two Cities: The novel opens with 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times', and is set in London and Paris in the French Revolution.
Dickens novels, by when serialization be.Great Expectations: Pip's rise from blacksmith's apprentice to gentleman is told here, and Dickens changed the ending after a friend suggested a happier one.
Dickens novels, by when serialization be.The Mystery of Edwin Drood: Dickens died in 1870 leaving this mystery half-finished, so no one knows for sure who killed, or if anyone did, the title character.

How much sweeter than table sugar?.Lactose (milk sugar): Lactose is the sugar of milk and is only about a third as sweet as table sugar, which is why many people can't digest it as adults.
How much sweeter than table sugar?.Glucose: Glucose circulates in your blood as blood sugar and is the main fuel for your brain, yet tastes noticeably less sweet than table sugar.
How much sweeter than table sugar?.Sucrose (table sugar): Sucrose is made of one glucose and one fructose joined together, and it comes mostly from sugar cane and sugar beet.
How much sweeter than table sugar?.Fructose: Fructose is the sweetest natural sugar and gives fruit and honey much of their sweetness, which is why high-fructose syrups are so popular in food.
How much sweeter than table sugar?.Cyclamate: Cyclamate was discovered by accident in 1937 when a chemist set a cigarette down in his lab and tasted its sweetness, and the US banned it in 1969.
How much sweeter than table sugar?.Aspartame: Aspartame was also found by accident, when chemist James Schlatter licked his finger while working on an ulcer drug, and it is made of two amino acids.
How much sweeter than table sugar?.Saccharin: Saccharin, found accidentally in 1879 by a chemist who noticed his bread tasted sweet, was the first artificial sweetener.
How much sweeter than table sugar?.Sucralose: Sucralose is made by swapping some atoms in sugar for chlorine, which the body cannot use, so it adds almost no calories.
How much sweeter than table sugar?.Neotame: Neotame is a chemical cousin of aspartame, but it is far stronger, and the tiny amounts needed make it very cheap to use.
How much sweeter than table sugar?.Advantame: Advantame is among the most intensely sweet sweeteners approved for food, and a sprinkle that is barely visible is enough to sweeten a drink.

Quick math: which answer is biggest?.Square root of 144: A dozen: twelve divides so many ways that the dozen survives in eggs and in the clock face.
Quick math: which answer is biggest?.100 ÷ 4: A quarter is the name of the US 25-cent coin, and it's why a 'quarter' of anything, from hours to pies, means one in four.
Quick math: which answer is biggest?.3 cubed: A Rubik's Cube looks like 27 little cubes in a 3 × 3 × 3 arrangement, though inside it is really a clever mechanism.
Quick math: which answer is biggest?.15% of 200: A tipping shortcut: take ten percent, then add half of that again, and you have 15% without a calculator.
Quick math: which answer is biggest?.6 × 7: Douglas Adams's Hitchhiker's Guide made 42 the 'answer to life, the universe and everything'.
Quick math: which answer is biggest?.9 × 6: In base 13, six times nine really does equal 42, though Adams said that was a coincidence.
Quick math: which answer is biggest?.7 × 8: A classic mnemonic: 56 = 7 × 8 follows the counting sequence 5, 6, 7, 8, which helps with a notoriously tricky fact.
Quick math: which answer is biggest?.A quarter of 260: 65 is the smallest number that can be written as the sum of two squares in two ways: 1 + 64 and 16 + 49.
Quick math: which answer is biggest?.11 × 11: Squares of 11 and 111 give palindromes, 121 and 12,321, a pattern that holds for the first few repunits only.
Quick math: which answer is biggest?.2 to the 8th power: A byte has 256 possible values, 0 to 255, so this number shows up all over computing and in colour channels.

Number of pins in these connectors.3.5 mm headphone plug (TRS): The 1/4 inch jack came from telephone switchboards in the 1870s, and the 3.5 mm version shrank for transistor radios.
Number of pins in these connectors.USB 2.0 Type-A: Four pins carry power, ground and two data lines; it famously never goes in the right way round at the first attempt.
Number of pins in these connectors.Lightning: Introduced in 2012 to replace the 30-pin dock, it was reversible, and EU rules later pushed Apple toward USB-C.
Number of pins in these connectors.VGA: IBM introduced it in 1987 with the PS/2, and its 15-pin D-shaped plug carried analogue video for decades.
Number of pins in these connectors.HDMI (Type A): One cable carries both video and audio, and it launched in 2003 to replace tangles of older connectors.
Number of pins in these connectors.DisplayPort: A VESA standard from 2006, it is HDMI's rival and can daisy-chain several monitors.
Number of pins in these connectors.SCART: This 21-pin connector linked European TVs and VCRs, and could carry RGB video for a sharper picture.
Number of pins in these connectors.USB-C: It's reversible, designed so there is no wrong way to plug it in, and one cable can handle power, data and video.
Number of pins in these connectors.PC printer parallel port: The 25-pin parallel port was how PCs talked to printers for years; the printer end used a different 36-pin plug.
Number of pins in these connectors.IDE hard drive cable: Later drive cables used 80 wires for faster speeds but kept the same 40-pin connector.

How old these rulers were when they took.Henry VI of England: He became king at nine months in 1422, and also nominally King of France, but later suffered bouts of mental illness.
How old these rulers were when they took.Tutankhamun: The boy-king took the throne around nine and died at about 18; his tomb, found in 1922, was largely intact.
How old these rulers were when they took.Nero: He became emperor at 16 in AD 54 after his mother's scheming, and ruled during the Great Fire of Rome in 64.
How old these rulers were when they took.Alexander the Great: He became king after his father Philip II was murdered in 336 BC, and the philosopher Aristotle had been his tutor.
How old these rulers were when they took.Caligula: His real name was Gaius, and 'Caligula' means 'little boots', a nickname soldiers gave him as a child in a tiny uniform.
How old these rulers were when they took.William the Conqueror: Duke of Normandy since childhood, he won the Battle of Hastings and was crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066.
How old these rulers were when they took.Kublai Khan: A grandson of Genghis Khan, he founded the Yuan dynasty, ruled China, and hosted Marco Polo according to Polo's own account.
How old these rulers were when they took.Claudius: According to the story, soldiers found him hiding behind a curtain after Caligula's murder and made him emperor; he conquered Britain.
How old these rulers were when they took.Tiberius: He succeeded Augustus, his stepfather, and spent his last decade living on the island of Capri.
How old these rulers were when they took.Galba: The first emperor in the Year of the Four Emperors, AD 69, he lasted only about seven months before being murdered.

When these metals were discovered.Cobalt: Georg Brandt isolated it, and it is named for kobold, the goblin miners blamed for ores that poisoned them.
When these metals were discovered.Nickel: Axel Cronstedt named it from kupfernickel, devil's copper, since the ore looked like copper ore but yielded none.
When these metals were discovered.Manganese: Johan Gahn isolated it, and it is essential for making steel, and in tiny amounts for the human body.
When these metals were discovered.Tungsten: The Elhuyar brothers isolated it; its symbol W comes from wolfram, and it melts at around 3,400 degrees Celsius, the highest of any metal.
When these metals were discovered.Titanium: William Gregor found it in Cornwall, and Klaproth named it for the Titans; it is as strong as steel but about 45 percent lighter.
When these metals were discovered.Chromium: Louis Vauquelin found it in Siberian red lead, and its name comes from the Greek word for color, because of its vivid compounds.
When these metals were discovered.Potassium: Humphry Davy isolated it by electrolysis of molten potash; it reacts violently with water, yet it is also in bananas.
When these metals were discovered.Lithium: Johan Arfwedson found it in a mineral from a Swedish island and named it from the Greek for stone; it now powers batteries.
When these metals were discovered.Aluminium: Hans Christian Ørsted first isolated it, and it was once so rare that Napoleon III reportedly served honored guests with aluminium cutlery.
When these metals were discovered.Gallium: Lecoq de Boisbaudran named it for France, Gallia; Mendeleev had predicted it, and it melts in your hand at about 30 degrees Celsius.

Typical weight of these vegetables.A single pea: Gregor Mendel's pea-plant crosses in the 1850s and 60s laid the groundwork for the science of genetics.
Typical weight of these vegetables.Garlic clove: Garlic's sharp smell comes from allicin, a compound that forms only when a clove is crushed, chopped or bitten.
Typical weight of these vegetables.Cherry tomato: Botanically a fruit, the tomato was once feared in Europe as poisonous because it belongs to the nightshade family.
Typical weight of these vegetables.Carrot: Early cultivated carrots were purple and yellow; the familiar orange kind is generally credited to Dutch growers in the 1600s.
Typical weight of these vegetables.Potato: Native to the Andes, potatoes come in thousands of varieties there, and reached Europe in the 1500s.
Typical weight of these vegetables.Eggplant: Botanically a berry, it got its English name from early white, egg-shaped varieties, and it is a nightshade like tomato and potato.
Typical weight of these vegetables.Head of cauliflower: Cauliflower, cabbage, broccoli and kale are all cultivars of one wild species, Brassica oleracea.
Typical weight of these vegetables.Butternut squash: Bred in Massachusetts in the 1940s, butternut squash sweetens in storage as its starch turns to sugar.
Typical weight of these vegetables.Carving pumpkin: Jack-o'-lanterns began as carved turnips in Ireland and Scotland; immigrants switched to pumpkins in North America.
Typical weight of these vegetables.World-record giant pumpkin: Growers coax these to over a tonne, and at peak growth a giant pumpkin can gain many kilograms in a single day.

Old and odd units of time.Jiffy: Chemist Gilbert Lewis proposed it as the time light takes to travel one foot, about a billionth of a second. In computing it means a clock tick.
Old and odd units of time.Moment (medieval): A medieval unit of 90 seconds, a tenth of an hour in the system where an hour had 40 moments. The word still survives in "wait a moment".
Old and odd units of time.Hour: Our 60-minute hour comes from Babylonian counting in sixties, the same habit that gave us 60-second minutes and the 360-degree circle.
Old and odd units of time.Sennight: An old word for a week, from "seven nights". Its relative, "fortnight", from "fourteen nights", is still used in British English.
Old and odd units of time.Fortnight: A contraction of "fourteen nights", still everyday speech in British English, where wages or rubbish collection may be fortnightly.
Old and odd units of time.Olympiad: The ancient Greek four-year cycle between Games, used to date events. Greeks counted time in Olympiads from 776 BC.
Old and odd units of time.Lustrum: A five-year period in ancient Rome, named for a purification ritual held after each census. Rarely used now, apart from showing off.
Old and odd units of time.Score: Twenty years, from an old counting-by-twenties habit. The Bible's "three score years and ten" gives a lifespan of 70, and Lincoln opened Gettysburg with one.
Old and odd units of time.Jubilee: In the Bible, every 50th year was a time of freedom and land return, but today the word marks celebrations, such as a monarch's 50th anniversary.
Old and odd units of time.Millennium: A thousand years. Many people wrongly celebrated the new one in 1999, but it actually began on January 1, 2001, since the calendar has no year zero.

African history before 1500, in order.Carthage founded (trad.): Tradition says Queen Dido founded this North African city, which later became Rome's great rival and was destroyed in 146 BC.
African history before 1500, in order.Meroë becomes Kush's capital: This city on the Nile, in what is now Sudan, became famed for iron-working, and it was home to a line of pyramid-building rulers.
African history before 1500, in order.Aksum's king turns Christian: Aksum's king Ezana adopted Christianity, making it one of the first states to do so, and it issued its own gold coins.
African history before 1500, in order.Vandals take Carthage: Germanic raiders captured the city, making it the capital of a kingdom that ruled North Africa for about a century.
African history before 1500, in order.Lalibela's rock churches: Lalibela's churches are carved downward from solid rock in Ethiopia, and they remain a place of pilgrimage today.
African history before 1500, in order.Mali Empire founded: Founded by Sundiata Keita, it grew rich on gold and salt and became one of the largest empires of its age.
African history before 1500, in order.Mansa Musa's hajj: The Mali emperor's pilgrimage to Mecca was so lavish that his gold gave prices in Cairo a lasting dip.
African history before 1500, in order.Kingdom of Kongo founded: This Central African kingdom grew along the Congo River, and its rulers later corresponded with Portugal's kings.
African history before 1500, in order.Sonni Ali expands Songhai: He turned a small Niger River state into a vast empire with a strong navy and its center in Gao.
African history before 1500, in order.Dias rounds the Cape: Bartolomeu Dias's voyage opened the sea route around Africa that Vasco da Gama would use to reach India.

How many members or seats?.G7 countries: The US, UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy and Japan; Russia was part of a G8 until 2014.
How many members or seats?.US Supreme Court justices: Congress sets the number, which has ranged from six to ten, and it has been nine since 1869.
How many members or seats?.UN Security Council: Five permanent members hold veto power, while ten others are elected for two-year terms.
How many members or seats?.EU member states: The union has had this many members since the United Kingdom left in 2020.
How many members or seats?.NATO members: Sweden became the newest member in 2024, joining a group started with 12 members in 1949.
How many members or seats?.US Senate: Two senators from each state; the Vice President casts a tiebreaking vote.
How many members or seats?.UN member states: South Sudan was the newest member, joining in 2011.
How many members or seats?.US House of Representatives: The number has been capped since the early 1900s, and is divided among states by population.
How many members or seats?.US Electoral College votes: A candidate needs 270 to win; it is 435 + 100 + 3 for the District of Columbia.
How many members or seats?.UK House of Commons: Its green-benched chamber seats only about 430, so MPs often have to stand during big debates.

Historic tsunamis, in order.Storegga slide (Norway): The huge undersea landslide off Norway triggered a giant wave that hit Scotland and Doggerland, and it is one of the largest known.
Historic tsunamis, in order.Crete earthquake: The earthquake destroyed Alexandria, and it threw ships far inland, and the event was recorded by the historian Ammianus Marcellinus.
Historic tsunamis, in order.Lisbon: The earthquake and fire also killed tens of thousands in Portugal's capital, and a tsunami struck soon after, and it changed European thinking.
Historic tsunamis, in order.Krakatoa: The volcanic eruption was heard thousands of kilometres away, and its tsunami killed more than 36,000 people in Indonesia.
Historic tsunamis, in order.Aleutian (April Fools'): The tsunami hit Hilo, Hawaii, and it led to the creation of the Pacific Tsunami Warning System.
Historic tsunamis, in order.Lituya Bay, Alaska: The mega-tsunami in the Alaska fjord reached 524 metres up the slope, and it is the tallest wave ever recorded.
Historic tsunamis, in order.Great Chilean: The most powerful earthquake ever recorded, of magnitude 9.5, sent a tsunami across the Pacific as far as Japan.
Historic tsunamis, in order.Good Friday (Alaska): The Alaskan earthquake was the second-largest ever recorded, and the tsunamis killed people as far as California.
Historic tsunamis, in order.Indian Ocean: The earthquake off Sumatra killed more than 200,000 people in a dozen countries, and it led to a global warning system.
Historic tsunamis, in order.Tōhoku, Japan: The earthquake and tsunami in Japan caused the Fukushima nuclear disaster, and it was the costliest natural disaster in history.

When these legends retired for good.Babe Ruth: He retired with 714 home runs, a record that stood until Hank Aaron broke it in 1974.
When these legends retired for good.Pele: He retired in 1977 after playing for the New York Cosmos, having won three World Cups.
When these legends retired for good.Muhammad Ali: Three-time heavyweight champion, he lost his final fight to Trevor Berbick in 1981.
When these legends retired for good.Wayne Gretzky: The NHL retired his number 99 across the entire league, and he holds records for goals and assists.
When these legends retired for good.Michael Jordan: He retired a third time in 2003 after playing for the Washington Wizards, having won six titles with Chicago.
When these legends retired for good.Michael Phelps: He retired with 28 Olympic medals, 23 of them gold, the most ever.
When these legends retired for good.Usain Bolt: He holds the 100 m world record of 9.58 seconds and the 200 m record of 19.19.
When these legends retired for good.Roger Federer: His last match was at London's Laver Cup, and he ended with 20 Grand Slam singles titles.
When these legends retired for good.Tom Brady: He won seven Super Bowls, more than any NFL franchise has.
When these legends retired for good.Rafael Nadal: He won a record 14 French Open titles, and his last event was the Davis Cup Finals.

French novels, by publication.Candide: Voltaire's satire mocks blind optimism and ends with the line that we must cultivate our garden.
French novels, by publication.Les Liaisons dangereuses: Told entirely through letters, it follows scheming aristocrats and inspired the films Dangerous Liaisons and Cruel Intentions.
French novels, by publication.The Red and the Black: Stendhal's novel follows ambitious Julien Sorel. The title is often read as the army and the Church, the era's two career paths.
French novels, by publication.The Hunchback of Notre-Dame: Victor Hugo's book helped spark a campaign to save and restore Paris's Notre-Dame cathedral, which had fallen into neglect.
French novels, by publication.The Count of Monte Cristo: Dumas serialized it in a newspaper. The tale of a wrongly jailed sailor's revenge was partly inspired by a real case.
French novels, by publication.Madame Bovary: Flaubert was put on trial for obscenity over this book in 1857, was acquitted, and the scandal boosted its fame.
French novels, by publication.Les Misérables: Hugo wrote much of it in exile on the island of Guernsey. It later became one of the world's longest-running musicals.
French novels, by publication.The Phantom of the Opera: Gaston Leroux took inspiration from real events at the Paris Opera, including a chandelier counterweight that fell in 1896.
French novels, by publication.The Stranger: Camus's novel opens with the line 'Maman died today'. He won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1957.
French novels, by publication.The Little Prince: Written by a pilot while in exile in New York, it is among the most translated books ever, in hundreds of languages.

When these odd deaths happened (as legen.Aeschylus: falling tortoise: The Greek playwright was said to have been killed when an eagle mistook his bald head for a rock and dropped a tortoise on it, though historians doubt it.
When these odd deaths happened (as legen.Chrysippus: died laughing: The Stoic philosopher supposedly died of laughter after watching a donkey eat figs, then asking for wine to wash them down.
When these odd deaths happened (as legen.Pliny the Elder: Vesuvius: The Roman writer and admiral sailed toward the eruption of Mount Vesuvius to rescue people, and died on the shore; Pompeii was buried.
When these odd deaths happened (as legen.Attila: nosebleed at wedding: The Hun leader reputedly died of a nosebleed on his wedding night, choking after heavy drinking, according to a Roman chronicler.
When these odd deaths happened (as legen.Sigurd: bitten by a dead foe: Earl Sigurd of Orkney tied a slain rival's head to his saddle; legend says its tooth grazed his leg, and the wound killed him.
When these odd deaths happened (as legen.Henry I: too many lampreys: Chronicles say Henry I of England died after eating a 'surfeit of lampreys', against his doctor's advice.
When these odd deaths happened (as legen.Adrian IV: choked on a fly: The only English pope, Nicholas Breakspear, reportedly choked on a fly in his wine, though the story is probably legend.
When these odd deaths happened (as legen.Barbarossa: drowned in a river: The Holy Roman Emperor drowned in the Saleph River while leading the Third Crusade, and his army largely fell apart afterward.
When these odd deaths happened (as legen.Martin of Aragon: laughing fit: The King of Aragon reportedly died laughing at a jester's joke, after a bout of indigestion, and left no heir.
When these odd deaths happened (as legen.Clarence: drowned in wine: The Duke of Clarence, brother of Edward IV, was reportedly drowned in a barrel of malmsey wine in the Tower of London.

Fairy tales and fables, by first printin.Puss in Boots (Perrault): Charles Perrault's tale of a clever cat who wins his master a kingdom helped establish the fairy-tale genre in French salons.
Fairy tales and fables, by first printin.Arabian Nights in French: Antoine Galland's translation introduced Europe to Aladdin and Ali Baba, though those two stories were added from other sources.
Fairy tales and fables, by first printin.Beauty and the Beast: Gabrielle-Suzanne de Villeneuve wrote the long original, and Disney's film draws on a shorter version by Madame de Beaumont.
Fairy tales and fables, by first printin.Hansel and Gretel (Grimm): The Brothers Grimm collected this tale of children abandoned in the woods, and the gingerbread house is a famous trap.
Fairy tales and fables, by first printin.The Nutcracker and Mouse King: E.T.A. Hoffmann's story inspired Tchaikovsky's ballet, which became a Christmas tradition.
Fairy tales and fables, by first printin.The Little Mermaid: Hans Christian Andersen's tale of a sea princess who gives up her voice originally ended sadly, unlike Disney's film.
Fairy tales and fables, by first printin.The Snow Queen: Andersen's tale of a mirror shard in a boy's heart inspired Disney's Frozen, and was among his longest stories.
Fairy tales and fables, by first printin.Pinocchio (as a book): Carlo Collodi's wooden puppet appeared first as a newspaper serial, and his nose grows with every lie in the book.
Fairy tales and fables, by first printin.The Happy Prince: Oscar Wilde's tale of a statue and a swallow was written for his sons, and ends with a quiet note of sacrifice.
Fairy tales and fables, by first printin.Peter Pan (the play): J.M. Barrie's play premiered in London, and the boy who wouldn't grow up was named after his friends' sons.

Canadian and US cities from north to sou.Iqaluit: The capital of Nunavut has no road to anywhere else, so everything arrives by plane or sea.
Canadian and US cities from north to sou.Whitehorse: The Yukon's capital on the Yukon River was a base for Klondike Gold Rush prospectors.
Canadian and US cities from north to sou.Edmonton: The northernmost city in North America with over a million people in its metro area, and home to West Edmonton Mall.
Canadian and US cities from north to sou.Winnipeg: Near the geographic centre of North America, it sits where the Red and Assiniboine rivers meet.
Canadian and US cities from north to sou.Seattle: Home to the Space Needle, it is the birthplace of Starbucks and Amazon, and Boeing built planes here.
Canadian and US cities from north to sou.Montreal: One of the world's largest French-speaking cities outside France.
Canadian and US cities from north to sou.Toronto: Canada's largest city; the CN Tower was the world's tallest freestanding structure from 1976 to 2007.
Canadian and US cities from north to sou.Chicago: Rebuilt after the 1871 fire, it saw the first skyscraper, the Home Insurance Building, rise in 1885.
Canadian and US cities from north to sou.New York: Perhaps the world's most linguistically diverse city, with hundreds of languages spoken.
The capital belongs to no state, and Pierre L'Enfant designed its street plan.

When these cookies and biscuits debuted.Fig Newtons: Named after the town of Newton, Massachusetts, this fig-jam-filled pastry bar was a Gilded Age invention that later became a lunchbox staple.
When these cookies and biscuits debuted.Barnum's Animal Crackers: The box was made with a string handle so it could hang from a Christmas tree, and it's still sold that way.
When these cookies and biscuits debuted.Oreo: Nabisco launched it four years after rival Hydrox, and for decades it was seen as the imitator before it became the bestseller.
When these cookies and biscuits debuted.Girl Scout Cookies: The first sales were in Muskogee, Oklahoma, when girls baked cookies at home; the troop sold them to raise funds.
When these cookies and biscuits debuted.Jaffa Cakes: A UK tax tribunal ruled in 1991 that it counts as a cake, not a biscuit, which saved the maker from paying VAT on it.
When these cookies and biscuits debuted.Lotus Biscoff: The caramelized Belgian spiced biscuit became a spread sensation, and airlines served it as an in-flight snack for years.
When these cookies and biscuits debuted.Pepperidge Farm Milano: Named after the Italian city, this cookie with a chocolate sandwich filling became a bestseller in the Pepperidge Farm lineup.
When these cookies and biscuits debuted.Tim Tam: Inspired by a British chocolate biscuit, it spawned the "Tim Tam Slam", where you sip a drink through two bitten corners.
When these cookies and biscuits debuted.Famous Amos: Wally Amos, a Hollywood talent agent, started this chocolate chip cookie brand, handing out cookies to celebrity friends.
When these cookies and biscuits debuted.Crumbl Cookies: This chain in Logan, Utah rotates its flavors weekly and sells them in a signature pink box.

Milestones in the history of English.Anglo-Saxons settle Britain: The Anglo-Saxons came from what is now Germany and Denmark, and their language, Old English, is the root of English.
Milestones in the history of English.Augustine brings Latin letters: Augustine arrived in Kent to convert the English, and Latin script gradually replaced runes for writing.
Milestones in the history of English.Viking raid on Lindisfarne: The raid on Lindisfarne began the Viking Age in England, and the Norse settlers left words such as sky, egg and knife.
Milestones in the history of English.Norman Conquest: After William conquered England, Norman French became the language of the elite, adding thousands of words like beef and judge.
Milestones in the history of English.English allowed in law courts: The Statute of Pleading made English the language of the courts, after years of French, though records were kept in Latin.
Milestones in the history of English.Caxton's printing press: William Caxton set up England's first printing press in Westminster, and his choices helped standardize spelling.
Milestones in the history of English.Jamestown colony founded: The first permanent English settlement in America, Jamestown, carried English words and speakers to the New World.
Milestones in the history of English.Shakespeare's First Folio: Seven years after Shakespeare died, his friends collected 36 of his plays, saving about half of them from being lost.
Milestones in the history of English.Johnson's Dictionary: Samuel Johnson spent nine years compiling it, mostly alone, and it defined 42,000 words with quotations.
Milestones in the history of English.OED completed: The OED took 70 years to complete, started in 1857, and its first editors were assisted by volunteers who mailed slips of quotations.

Shock upsets through the years.USA beats England, World Cup: Joe Gaetjens, a Haitian-born player, scored with a diving header in Belo Horizonte, and England's stars went home stunned.
Shock upsets through the years.Clay beats Liston: Cassius Clay was a heavy underdog, but Liston stayed on his stool before round seven; Clay soon announced his new name, Muhammad Ali.
Shock upsets through the years.Jets win Super Bowl III: Joe Namath guaranteed victory days before, then led the underdog Jets past the Baltimore Colts, who were favoured by about 18 points.
Shock upsets through the years.Buster Douglas KOs Tyson: Tyson was undefeated and unbeaten for years; the Tokyo bookmakers' odds on Douglas were about 42 to 1.
Shock upsets through the years.Denmark wins the Euros: Denmark only entered after Yugoslavia was excluded, with players recalled from holiday, and then beat Germany 2-0 in the final.
Shock upsets through the years.Rulon Gardner beats Karelin: Karelin, a Greco-Roman wrestling giant, had not lost in 13 years until the American farmer from Wyoming beat him in Sydney.
Shock upsets through the years.Greece wins the Euros: Otto Rehhagel's Greece were rank outsiders at the start, then beat hosts Portugal 1-0 in the final with a header from Angelos Charisteas.
Shock upsets through the years.Japan stuns South Africa: Karne Hesketh's last-minute try won 34-32 in Brighton and is known simply as the Miracle of Brighton.
Shock upsets through the years.Leicester win the league: Bookmakers offered 5,000 to 1 on Leicester at the start of the season, and they clinched the title when Tottenham drew with Chelsea.
Shock upsets through the years.UMBC beats Virginia: A 16th seed had lost all 135 previous games against a 1 seed in the men's tournament before UMBC won 74-54.

Australian animals by weight.Honey possum: It feeds entirely on nectar and pollen, using a brush-tipped tongue, and is a pollinator of banksias.
Australian animals by weight.Sugar glider: It glides up to about 50 metres between trees using a skin membrane.
Australian animals by weight.Laughing kookaburra: Its 'laughing' call is a territorial chorus, and the bird eats snakes.
Australian animals by weight.Platypus: Males have a venomous spur on their hind legs, and the animal lays eggs despite being a mammal.
Australian animals by weight.Short-beaked echidna: This egg-laying mammal has spines and a baby called a puggle.
Australian animals by weight.Koala: It sleeps up to 20 hours a day, as eucalyptus leaves give little energy, and its fingerprints look strikingly like ours.
Australian animals by weight.Dingo: The Dingo Fence, among the longest structures on Earth, was built partly to keep it from sheep country.
Australian animals by weight.Emu: In 1932 the Australian army lost the Emu War against it in Western Australia.
Australian animals by weight.Red kangaroo (male): The largest marsupial can hop at about 70 km/h and leap several metres in a bound.
Australian animals by weight.Saltwater crocodile (male): The largest living reptile has the strongest bite force measured in any animal, and males can reach about six metres.

Palme d'Or winners at Cannes.The Third Man: The Third Man won the Grand Prix, then the top prize at Cannes, in 1949. Its zither score by Anton Karas was a massive hit.
Palme d'Or winners at Cannes.Taxi Driver: Martin Scorsese's Taxi Driver won in 1976, and its line You talking to me? comes from an ad-libbed scene by Robert De Niro.
Palme d'Or winners at Cannes.Apocalypse Now: Apocalypse Now won in 1979, while director Francis Ford Coppola was still finishing the film, famously after a troubled shoot in the Philippines.
Palme d'Or winners at Cannes.Sex, Lies, and Videotape: Steven Soderbergh's debut won in 1989, helping launch the indie film boom, and he was only 26.
Palme d'Or winners at Cannes.Pulp Fiction: Quentin Tarantino's film won in 1994, and its non-linear story helped turn Tarantino into a household name.
Palme d'Or winners at Cannes.Fahrenheit 9/11: Michael Moore's documentary won in 2004, and it was the first documentary to win since 1956.
Palme d'Or winners at Cannes.The Tree of Life: Terrence Malick's film won in 2011, and its cosmic creation sequence helped it stand out from the rest.
Palme d'Or winners at Cannes.Parasite: Bong Joon-ho's film became the first South Korean film to win the Palme d'Or, and it went on to win Best Picture at the Oscars.
Palme d'Or winners at Cannes.Titane: Julia Ducournau's body-horror film made her only the second woman to win the Palme d'Or, after Jane Campion in 1993.
Palme d'Or winners at Cannes.Anatomy of a Fall: Justine Triet's courtroom drama made her the third woman to win the Palme d'Or, and its dog Messi won a Palm Dog award.

South and Southeast Asian countries by a.Singapore: Singapore is a city-state that has grown by about a quarter through land reclamation. It imports sand to keep expanding.
South and Southeast Asian countries by a.Brunei: Brunei is an oil-rich sultanate on Borneo, split into two parts by Malaysia. Its sultan lives in one of the world's largest palaces.
South and Southeast Asian countries by a.Timor-Leste: Timor-Leste became independent in 2002, one of the world's newest nations. Portuguese and Tetum are its official languages.
South and Southeast Asian countries by a.Bangladesh: Bangladesh is among the most densely populated countries, and it lies on the vast Ganges-Brahmaputra delta. It's about the size of Iowa.
South and Southeast Asian countries by a.Cambodia: Cambodia is home to Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument in the world. It appears on the national flag.
South and Southeast Asian countries by a.Laos: Landlocked Laos is known for the Plain of Jars, with thousands of mysterious stone jars. The Mekong river forms much of its border.
South and Southeast Asian countries by a.Vietnam: Vietnam's S-shaped coastline runs over 3,000 km. It is one of the largest coffee producers in the world.
South and Southeast Asian countries by a.Thailand: Thailand is the only country in Southeast Asia that was never colonised by a European power. Its name means "land of the free."
South and Southeast Asian countries by a.Myanmar: Myanmar, formerly Burma, is the largest mainland Southeast Asian country. Its Bagan plain holds thousands of ancient temples.
South and Southeast Asian countries by a.Indonesia: Indonesia is the world's largest archipelago, with over 17,000 islands. It sits on the Ring of Fire, with many volcanoes.

Ancient inventions, oldest first.Pottery: Fragments found in a cave in China suggest pots were made long before farming. Early potters used them to cook and store.
Ancient inventions, oldest first.Farming: Wheat and barley were farmed first in the Fertile Crescent of the Middle East. Settling down to farm led to villages and cities.
Ancient inventions, oldest first.Wheeled vehicles: Wheeled vehicles appeared in Mesopotamia and Europe at about the same time. The first wheels were likely used for pottery, not travel.
Ancient inventions, oldest first.Cuneiform writing: Sumerians pressed wedge-shaped marks into clay with a reed stylus. It began as bookkeeping for grain and livestock.
Ancient inventions, oldest first.Coins (Lydia): Lydia, in modern Turkey, struck the first coins from electrum, a natural gold-silver alloy. The idea quickly spread through the Greek world.
Ancient inventions, oldest first.Antikythera mechanism: Found in a Greek shipwreck in 1901, this geared device predicted eclipses and tracked the Olympic cycle. It's often called the earliest analogue computer.
Ancient inventions, oldest first.Paper (Cai Lun): Cai Lun was a court official of China's Han dynasty. He is credited with making paper from bark, rags and old fishing nets.
Ancient inventions, oldest first.Gunpowder: Chinese alchemists seeking an elixir of life stumbled on gunpowder. It took centuries to spread west.
Ancient inventions, oldest first.Movable type (Bi Sheng): Bi Sheng carved individual characters in baked clay, centuries before Europe's printing. It was not widely adopted since Chinese has thousands of characters.
Ancient inventions, oldest first.Gutenberg press: Johannes Gutenberg's Mainz workshop printed the Bible with metal type and a press adapted from wine presses. Around 180 copies were made.

Main RAM in classic machines.Atari 2600: Its 128 bytes of RAM couldn't even hold a full screen image. Programmers "raced the beam," updating graphics line by line.
Main RAM in classic machines.Sinclair ZX81: Clive Sinclair's tiny, cheap computer had just 1 KB of memory. It sold over a million and introduced many Britons to programming.
Main RAM in classic machines.NES: The NES had just 2 KB of main memory, but cartridges added extra chips. That is how Super Mario Bros. squeezed in so much.
Main RAM in classic machines.Commodore 64: Its name comes from its memory size, and it's the best-selling single computer model of all time. Its sound chip was famous.
Main RAM in classic machines.Original Macintosh: The original Mac was launched with a Super Bowl ad in 1984. Its 128 KB was too tight, so a 512 KB model followed.
Main RAM in classic machines.Amiga 500: Commodore's 1987 machine was a favourite for games and music. It ran with a powerful graphics and sound chipset.
Main RAM in classic machines.PlayStation: Sony's 1994 console had only 2 MB of main memory, plus 1 MB of video memory. It beat Sega and Nintendo in sales.
Main RAM in classic machines.Nintendo 64: Its 4 MB could be doubled with an Expansion Pak. Donkey Kong 64 required the add-on.
Main RAM in classic machines.Xbox 360: The 360 shared 512 MB of memory between the CPU and graphics. It was released in 2005, with the first online console game service.
Main RAM in classic machines.PlayStation 4: It has 8 GB, which is some 64 million times more than the Atari. It launched in 2013 and sold over 100 million.

Man-made elements, by when they were fir.Technetium: Its name means 'artificial' in Greek; it was the first element made by humans, and it is used in medical scans.
Man-made elements, by when they were fir.Neptunium: Named after Neptune, following uranium, it was the first transuranium element, found at Berkeley.
Man-made elements, by when they were fir.Curium: Glenn Seaborg's team made it in 1944 and he first revealed it on a children's radio quiz show.
Man-made elements, by when they were fir.Einsteinium: A tiny sample glows from its radioactivity and decays quickly, so it has almost no use outside research.
Man-made elements, by when they were fir.Mendelevium: Atom-by-atom production in its first experiment yielded just 17 atoms.
Man-made elements, by when they were fir.Lawrencium: Named for Ernest Lawrence, who invented the cyclotron.
Man-made elements, by when they were fir.Seaborgium: Its 1974 discovery was claimed by both Berkeley and a Soviet team at Dubna.
Man-made elements, by when they were fir.Meitnerium: Named for Lise Meitner, who helped explain nuclear fission yet missed out on the Nobel Prize.
Man-made elements, by when they were fir.Copernicium: Made at the GSI lab in Darmstadt, Germany, which has found several elements.
Man-made elements, by when they were fir.Tennessine: Named for Tennessee, where Oak Ridge National Laboratory supplied the target material.

Leaves from minuscule to massive.Wolffia frond: Wolffia is the world's smallest flowering plant, a floating green dot rarely over a millimetre across. It has no roots and sometimes feeds people as watermeal.
Leaves from minuscule to massive.Duckweed frond: Duckweed can double its mass in a day or two in good conditions, covering ponds in green. It is also a protein-rich food for fish and ducks.
Leaves from minuscule to massive.Clover leaflet: Three leaflets make the usual clover leaf, and a four-leaf one is a rare mutation, found in roughly one clover in 10,000, which is why it counts as lucky.
Leaves from minuscule to massive.Holly leaf: The spiky leaves are mostly a defence against browsing animals, and higher leaves on the same tree are often smooth, since deer can't reach them.
Leaves from minuscule to massive.Oak leaf: Oak leaves are lobed and tough, and they hang on through winter in some species. Their tannins slow decay, so oak litter breaks down slowly.
Leaves from minuscule to massive.Fig leaf: Large and deeply lobed, the fig leaf is the famous cover-up in Genesis. Many Renaissance statues were later given plaster ones for modesty.
Leaves from minuscule to massive.Monstera leaf: The holes and splits in its leaves may help it let rain and light through to lower leaves in the rainforest. Fans call it the Swiss cheese plant.
Leaves from minuscule to massive.Banana leaf: Giant, flexible and waterproof, banana leaves serve as plates and cooking wraps in much of Asia and Latin America. Technically a banana plant is a huge herb, not a tree.
Leaves from minuscule to massive.Giant water lily pad: The Amazonian Victoria water lily has pads that can hold a small child's weight, thanks to a ribbed, spiny underside. It inspired the design of the Crystal Palace.
Leaves from minuscule to massive.Raffia palm leaf: Raffia palms hold the record for the longest leaves in the plant kingdom. Their fibres are used to make baskets and hats, as well as the raffia used in crafts.

Making risotto, step by step.Soften onion in butter: A classic risotto starts with a soffritto of finely chopped onion cooked slowly in butter or oil without browning, building a sweet base.
Making risotto, step by step.Toast the rice: Stirring the dry rice in fat until the grains turn translucent at the edges is called tostatura. It helps keep the grains firm.
Making risotto, step by step.Splash in white wine: Wine adds acidity that balances the richness. It is stirred until it evaporates, which leaves behind its flavour.
Making risotto, step by step.Add a ladle of hot stock: Stock is kept simmering so that it doesn't cool the rice. Carnaroli, Arborio and Vialone Nano are the classic Italian rice varieties.
Making risotto, step by step.Stir until it's absorbed: Stirring rubs starch from the grains, which gives risotto its creamy texture. The rice is cooked in stages, not simply boiled.
Making risotto, step by step.Keep adding stock: Add stock one ladle at a time, and wait until the previous one is absorbed. The process takes about 18 to 20 minutes in all.
Making risotto, step by step.Check rice is al dente: Rice should be tender on the outside with a slight firmness at the centre. Italian chefs say a good risotto should be all'onda, or wavy, like a wave.
Making risotto, step by step.Take off the heat: Stop cooking just before the rice is done, as the grains will carry on softening. The next step must be done off the heat.
Making risotto, step by step.Beat in butter and parmesan: This final beating is called mantecatura. Cold butter and cheese are whipped in vigorously to make the risotto glossy and creamy.
Making risotto, step by step.Rest, then serve: Letting the risotto sit for a minute or two lets the flavours settle. It should be served immediately, as it thickens quickly on the plate.
